title: Electronic Responses in Solid Oxygen with Coexisting Structural and Magnetic Orders
authors: Naomichi Sato, Makoto Naka, Joji Nasu
abstract: Solid oxygen provides a unique platform for studying the interplay between structural and magnetic degrees of freedom, as each O$_2$ molecule possesses an $S=1$ spin and weak intermolecular van der Waals interactions allow substantial structural flexibility. In addition, because of its small intermolecular hopping integrals, this system is known to be a strongly correlated electron system with a multiorbital nature. In this study, we examine electronic states and magnetic and dielectric responses using a multiorbital Hubbard model with Peierls-type electron-lattice coupling. This model provides a minimal description of the interplay between structural and magnetic degrees of freedom in solid oxygen. We apply the Hartree-Fock approximation to obtain the ground-state phase diagram. Antiferromagnetic order appears when the onsite Coulomb interaction is strong, whereas three nonmagnetic bond-ordered states emerge when it is weak. At intermediate interaction strengths, antiferromagnetic order coexists with each of the three bond orders. These three coexistence phases all break time-reversal symmetry; one preserves spatial inversion symmetry, whereas the other two also break it. The two inversion-breaking phases exhibit linear magnetoelectric responses, whereas the inversion-symmetric phase exhibits altermagnetic spin splitting and a piezomagnetic response. These responses may provide experimental signatures of coexisting magnetic and structural orders in high-pressure solid oxygen suggested by recent experiments.
summary: This theoretical study models solid oxygen using a multiorbital Hubbard model to explore the competition between magnetic and structural ordering. By applying the Hartree-Fock approximation, the authors map out a phase diagram predicting multiple coexistence states. These states are characterized by unique symmetry-breaking patterns that manifest as measurable responses like magnetoelectric or piezomagnetic effects, offering guidance for high-pressure experiments.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex interplay between structural (bond ordering) and magnetic degrees of freedom in solid oxygen, particularly focusing on how their coexistence breaks symmetries and generates measurable electronic responses.
main_result: The model predicts multiple coexistence phases where antiferromagnetism coexists with three distinct bond orders; these phases exhibit measurable responses like linear magnetoelectric or piezomagnetic effects.
method: The research employs the Hartree-Fock approximation applied to a multiorbital Hubbard model incorporating Peierls-type electron-lattice coupling.
model_or_system: The system is solid oxygen ($	ext{O}_2$), modeled using a multiorbital Hubbard Hamiltonian that includes onsite Coulomb repulsion, hopping terms, and electron-lattice coupling. The analysis is performed on a simplified two-dimensional square lattice representation.
key_observables: Electronic states, magnetic responses, dielectric responses, bond order parameters ($\Delta_Z, \Delta_M, \Delta_T$), and magnetoelectric/piezomagnetic coefficients ($\alpha_{xx'}$).
important_parameters: Onsite Coulomb interaction strength ($U$), Hund's coupling ($J_H$), and lattice distortion parameters ($p$ for pressure anisotropy).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hartree-Fock approximation, neglects pair-hopping terms, and often simplifies the structure to a 2D square lattice, ignoring full 3D stacking effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the square-lattice structure, the definition of molecular orbitals, the phase diagram showing AFM/bond order coexistence, and the dependence of the piezomagnetic response on applied uniaxial pressure.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the Hamiltonian, applies the Hartree-Fock method to map the ground-state phase diagram, and then calculates specific responses (magnetoelectric, piezomagnetic) by introducing external perturbations like strain or pressure anisotropy.
why_interesting: The detailed mapping of symmetry breaking (T, P, PT) in response to competing orders (magnetic vs. structural) provides a rich theoretical framework for understanding emergent quantum phenomena in correlated materials.
